title: “A Perverse Sort of Compassion” and the Point of Strong Teacher-Student Relationships
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens with a Finnish teacher, Heikki Vuorinen, who deliberately limits his empathy for refugee and immigrant students because too much sympathy would lead him to inflate marks for weak work. Stuart uses this to push back on the common idea that a great teacher is simply one with deep, caring relationships with every student. He argues that excessive empathy becomes a perverse compassion that puts adolescents' immediate needs ahead of their long-term growth, while the cold, cynical teacher is the opposite failure. The move he makes is to reframe the purpose of relationships: they exist so that the point of the classroom, students growing as thinkers, readers, writers, and people, can actually happen, not merely to ease classroom management. He closes with John Hattie's argument that a warm climate matters mainly because it lets students admit error and not-knowing without ridicule.
points: Teacher empathy has a failure mode: feeling students' hardships too strongly leads to lowered standards, such as better marks for worse work, which hurts the students who most need rigor.
The cynical Teacher Who Doesn't Care is a caricature that tempts well-meaning teachers into the opposite error of equating love with availability and rescue.
Strong relationships are a means to long-term flourishing and learning, not an end, and not only a classroom-management tool.
Hattie's point supplies the test: does the class climate let students say they do not understand without sneers from peers?
quotes: I don’t want to have too much empathy for [my students] because I have to teach. If I thought about all of this too much, I would give better marks to them for worse work.

This latter problem fools too many of us teachers into thinking we are awesome at our jobs simply because we have deep, caring relationships with every one of our students. When a kid comes in to chat for two hours after school, we think, “Yes, I am amazing!

But what I’m saying is that Vuorinen is wise, and there is such a thing as too much empathy for our students. If I felt my kids’ pain and heartbreak too strongly, I know myself enough to know that, like Vuorinen says, I would end up giving “better marks for worse work,” and I would end up thinking “Oh, you poor kid. Oh, well, what can I do?” Too much empathy would lead me to mail it in on the very kids who most need me not to mail it in.

The reason part of our job is to build strong relationships with kids is not solely to make classroom management easier; it’s to make the point of classrooms happen. We’re not simply trying to have connections with kids so that they don’t hurt themselves or others, but rather so that they won’t graduate from high school with lives devoid of joy, purpose, autonomy, and contribution.

So often, we are concerned about the classroom climate, but forget the purpose of warm, trustworthy, empathetic climates. The primary purpose is to allow students to feel okay about making mistakes and not knowing, and to establish a climate in which we welcome error as opportunities.
While teachers may have warm interpersonal interactions, this is not the point. The point is: do the students believe that the climate of the class is fair, empathetic, and trustworthy?
